gilman-herland-1915:
Charlotte Perkins Gilman published Herland in 1915, in her own magazine, The Forerunner. The novel imagines a country cut off from the world for two thousand years, where no men live. Gilman was a leading feminist thinker, and fiction let her test her ideas in story form.

Three male explorers, a rich playboy, a doctor, and a sociologist narrator, stumble into the hidden land. They find a peaceful, prosperous society of women who reproduce without men and raise children as a shared duty. The visitors' assumptions about women collapse one by one. Herland founded feminist speculative fiction and still reads as a bold thought experiment about gender and power.
dreiser-genius-1915:
Theodore Dreiser published The 'Genius' in 1915, his most autobiographical novel. Its hero is an artist rather than a financier, but the driving appetites are pure Dreiser. The book was attacked as obscene and effectively suppressed for years, with Dreiser's publisher too frightened to fight for it.

Eugene Witla climbs from a small Illinois town to New York success as an illustrator and painter. Fame and money feed a restless erotic life that wrecks his marriage and, at last, his art. Dreiser writes his own hungers into Witla with unusual nakedness, in long brooding passages on beauty and desire. The suppression fight made the novel a famous case for free expression. It remains his most personal work.
cather-song-of-the-lark-1915:
Willa Cather published The Song of the Lark in 1915, her third novel. Its heroine is Thea Kronborg, the daughter of a Swedish pastor in a small Colorado railroad town. Thea has a fine singing voice, and the novel follows her long climb toward a career in opera.

Thea studies in Chicago, works in church choirs, and slowly learns what art demands. Time in the cliff dwellings of Arizona helps her grasp the depth of her calling. At last she reaches the stage as a leading singer in New York. Cather shaped the novel as a study of talent, discipline, and the cost of becoming an artist.
hoffmann-devils-elixir-vol1-1815:
E. T. A. Hoffmann published The Devil's Elixir in German in 1815, and R. P. Gillies translated it into English in 1824. Volume one follows Brother Medardus, a Capuchin monk tempted by a relic said to be an elixir of the Devil. One taste breaks his vows and starts his ruin.

Medardus flees the monastery into crime, disguise, and a haunting double who shares his face. Love, murder, and madness crowd the road as his past hunts him down. Hoffmann mixes Gothic horror with sharp irony about faith and desire. The novel became a founding study of the double in modern fiction. Its wild plot still grips readers who like their tales dark.
hoffmann-devils-elixir-vol2-1815:
Volume two of The Devil's Elixir brings Hoffmann's monk novel to its close, in R. P. Gillies's translation of 1824. Medardus, worn by crime and pursuit, faces the full truth of his family's curse. The double who has dogged him steps out of rumor into plain sight.

Confession, trial, and penance take the place of flight and disguise. Hoffmann untangles the knot of births, sins, and mistaken selves that drove the tale. The ending weighs guilt against grace in a haunted, Catholic frame. Read with volume one, the novel stands complete: a Gothic landmark on the divided self. Its fevered method later fed Poe, Stevenson, and many more.
bonaventure-life-of-st-francis-1915:
Bonaventure, minister general of the Franciscans, wrote the Legenda Maior, the official life of Saint Francis of Assisi, around 1260. The order then ordered older lives destroyed, and his became the one true tale. Miss Lockhart translated the Latin into English in 1915. Bonaventure is the Seraphic Doctor, and his Francis is a mystic's portrait.

The life moves from Francis's wild youth to his conversion, the founding of the order, and the stigmata on La Verna. Miracles crowd the later chapters, told as signs of a soul made like Christ. Bonaventure writes theology in story form: Francis as the pattern of the gospel life. The book shaped how the West pictures its most loved saint.
campis-sendbrieff-1615:
Julianus de Campis wrote his Sendbrieff, a German open letter, in 1615. Its long title offers a report to all who had heard of the new brotherhood of the Rose Cross. The Rosicrucian Fama, a short manifesto, had just stirred print debate across German lands.

Campis writes as one of the first printed voices to answer that manifesto in public. His letter shows how fast the news of a hidden brotherhood could spread and excite hope. The pamphlet is a first-hand record of the furor of 1614 to 1616. Historians of the Rose Cross still start with texts like this one.
cantor-transfinite-numbers-jourdain-1915:
Georg Cantor created set theory and the mathematics of infinity in papers gathered here in English. Philip E. B. Jourdain translated Contributions to the Founding of the Theory of Transfinite Numbers in 1915. Jourdain also supplied an introduction and notes for new readers. Cantor's transfinite numbers measure sizes of sets that never end.

He proved that some infinities are larger than others, a result that shocked his peers. The counting numbers form one level, the points on a line a greater one. Cantor builds his cardinals and ordinals with great care. Many leading mathematicians at first resisted the work. It now anchors the foundations of mathematics. Jourdain's edition made it open to English readers.
sombart-quintessence-capitalism-epstein-:
Werner Sombart studied the modern businessman in The Quintessence of Capitalism, translated by M. Epstein in 1915. Dutton published the English edition in New York. Sombart asks what spirit drives the builders of modern business. He treats that capitalist spirit as a product of history, not of nature.

Bourgeois virtues and bold venture meet in his portrait of the type. Thrift, calculation, and daring combine in changing measure across the centuries. The book crowns the German historical school of economics in English. Sombart's answers differ sharply from Marx's, though both stress history. Readers meet a rich psychology of enterprise. Its portraits still provoke debate.
veblen-imperial-germany-1915:
Veblen applied his institutional method to a nation in Imperial Germany and the Industrial Revolution, from 1915. Germany had taken up machine industry late and fast. Its dynastic state, with an emperor and a military caste, ruled over that new industry. The mix of old power and new plant is Veblen's subject.

He asks what such a mix means for war, trade, and social change. Germany borrowed technology whole, skipping the slow habits England grew through. That borrowed edge, plus dynastic aims, made a dangerous compound in his analysis. The book appeared while Europe was already at war. It reads as institutional study turned on national growth.
ricardo-essay-profits-1815:
Ricardo's Essay on the Influence of a Low Price of Corn on the Profits of Stock appeared in 1815. The short name is the Essay on Profits. Corn meant grain, and its price governed wages across the economy. Ricardo builds a spare model farm economy to trace the effects.

Cheap corn lowers wages, raises profits, and shifts income among classes, in his model. That corn model became the core of his later Principles of Political Economy. The text here comes from McCulloch's 1846 edition of Ricardo's Works. Landowners and manufacturers fought over corn laws with his ideas as weapons. The essay shows his method at its purest.
spr-proceedings-vol27-1914-1915:
Parts sixty eight through seventy form volume twenty seven, spanning 1914 and 1915. War breaks over Europe in the middle of this volume's years. The Society for Psychical Research keeps publishing through the first shock. Telepathy work and trance sittings continue on the record.

Soldiers' and families' strange experiences begin to color the case files. Apparitions of the fallen would soon fill the society's postbag. Mediumship reports hold their long, checked form amid the change. Volume twenty seven catches the archive as the old world ends. The debate of 1882 to 1930 gains a wartime chapter here. Its tone stays measured against the times.
spr-proceedings-vol28-1915:
Volume twenty eight, dated 1915, consists of part seventy one alone. War now shapes every society meeting behind the printed page. The Society for Psychical Research still prints its evidence in full. Trance sittings and telepathy reports take their usual careful shape.

Cases touched by the fighting reach the files with the old standards applied. Names, dates, and witnesses stand checked as in peacetime. The society's refusal to lower its bar is the volume's quiet point. It forms one wartime brick in the long archive wall. Later volumes would face the flood of bereaved sitters. Here the record stays spare and firm. Judgment is left, as always, open.
stendhal-on-love-woolf-1915:
Stendhal tried to explain how love grows in On Love, the treatise the Woolfs translated in 1915. His famous word for the process is crystallization. The mind decks the beloved in perfections, as a bare branch left in a salt mine comes out coated in diamonds. The image anchors his whole theory of love.

Drawing on tales from Italy and his own keen watching, Stendhal sorts love into kinds and traces its birth, doubts, and hopes. The essay made him a founder of the psychology of love in fiction as well as theory. Novel readers still open it to see how the author of great romances thought love works.
young-journal-of-discourses-vol15:
Volume XV of the Journal of Discourses, issued at Liverpool in 1873, gathers sermons from a church deep into its Utah era. Brigham Young, his counsellors, and the Twelve Apostles preach across its many pages in turn. Their words went from shorthand notebooks to print abroad, then back to readers across the world.

Faith, conduct, and community fill the talks in the Journal's usual close mixture of high and daily things. Because nothing was smoothed for later tastes, the record stays a primary source of the first rank. Volume XV carries the doctrinal story forward by one more year of the movement's own voice.
roth-an-inquiry-into-the-animism-and-fol:
Walter Edmund Roth, a government ethnologist in British Guiana, set out to study the spirit beliefs of its native peoples in full. His 1915 inquiry, published by the Bureau of American Ethnology, treats animism as a system worth taking seriously.

Roth examines beliefs about the soul, its journeys during sleep and after death, and the spirits of animals, plants, and places. He gives long attention to kanaima, the feared practice of ritual killing and revenge. Myths, charms, and shamans' rites fill out the account. The study's order and patience made it a standard work on South American belief.
ford-good-soldier-1915:
Ford Madox Ford called his 1915 novel the saddest story, and its first line says so outright. The Good Soldier tells of two rich couples, English and American, whose orderly lives of spas and seasons hide adultery, lies, and quiet ruin.

John Dowell, the American husband, narrates years later, still unsure what he knew and when he knew it. His unreliability is the novel's engine: every calm scene returns darker on a second reading. Ford's impressionist method here taught modern fiction how to lie beautifully. The book is now widely held to be his masterpiece and one of the great English novels.
conrad-within-tides-1915:
Within the Tides, published in 1915, gathers four of Conrad's late stories, written as his powers and the Europe he knew both darkened. Three of the tales turn to the sea and the eastern ports of his youth.

'The Planter of Malata' follows a planter undone by obsessive love on his island. 'The Partner' is a grim tale of insurance fraud and a wrecked ship. 'The Inn of the Two Witches' moves to Spain for a story of murder and superstition, and 'Because of the Dollars' returns to eastern seas. The collection shows a master in his late, somber manner.
kafka-die-verwandlung-1915:
Die Verwandlung, published in 1915, is Kafka's novella in the original German: The Metamorphosis. Gregor Samsa, a traveling salesman, wakes one morning to find himself changed into a huge insect, and his family's horror becomes the story.

Told in calm, exact prose, the tale follows Gregor's shrinking place in the flat, his sister's turn from care to disgust, and his quiet death. Kafka never explains the change, which is the point: the absurd is treated as fact. This Kurt Wolff era text is the founding work of the literature of alienation, read here in the language Kafka wrote.
croce-hegel-living-dead-1915:
What Is Living and What Is Dead of the Philosophy of Hegel, published in English in 1915, is Croce's critical rescue of the German master. Croce had passed through Hegelianism himself; this book sorts what survives the system from what must be left behind.

Living, he finds, is Hegel's sense of thought as concrete and historical, his doctrine of opposites driving development. Dead is the system-building vanity: nature and history forced into triads by formula. The sorting is brisk, learned, and unsentimental. The book shaped how the twentieth century read Hegel, in Italy and far beyond it.
plos-pone-0003415:
Jesper Ryge and colleagues profiled gene activity in rodent spinal cord cells in this 2008 paper. Brain studies often read gene patterns from whole chunks of tissue. That mixes many cell types into one blurred signal. The team instead separated two distinct groups of nerve cells first.

Gene chips then read which genes each group had switched on. The two profiles differed in clear and useful ways. Together they form a molecular fingerprint for each cell group. Such profiles help researchers study how the cord handles movement and feeling. Other teams can reuse the profiles when they study single cell types.
plos-pone-0003515:
Konrad U. Foerstner and co-authors hunted drug-making genes in environmental DNA in this 2008 paper. Polyketides are natural products behind many antibiotics and medicines. Giant enzymes called polyketide synthases build them step by step. The team focused on the type I subgroup of those enzymes.

They screened metagenomic shotgun data with a computational method. The screen estimated how often these synthase genes occur in nature. Finding them in raw habitat DNA skips culturing microbes first. Each hit is a lead toward tomorrow's medicines. Most microbes cannot be grown in labs, so DNA screens are often the only route.
plos-pone-0003615:
Kaisa Silander and co-authors compared heart disease genetics by sex in this 2008 study. Cardiovascular disease rates and burden differ markedly between women and men. Lifestyle factors differ too, but they do not fully explain the gaps. Genetic risk profiles offered another place to look.

The team found those genetic profiles differ between the sexes. Some variants mattered more for women, others for men. Sex-aware risk scoring may predict heart disease better. Prevention plans could likewise be tuned by genetic sex differences. Heart disease is the top killer of both sexes in most rich countries.
plos-pone-0003715:
M. Corrie Schoeman and David S. Jacobs published this bat ecology study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Insect-eating bats live long, breed slowly, and face few predators. Forces like competition should therefore shape their communities strongly. So might the defenses of the insects they hunt.

Working in southern Africa, the authors weighed competition against prey defenses as shapers of bat ensembles. They compared the body and wing forms found together at sites with what each force predicts. The study tests which pressure, rivalry or prey armor, does more to decide which bats share a night sky.
plos-pone-0003815:
Jacqueline R. Weissman, Richard I. Kelley, Margaret L. Bauman, and colleagues published this cohort study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Earlier reports linked autism spectrum disorders with faults in mitochondrial energy production. One study claimed children with both diagnoses look just like other autistic children. Careful clinical data were scarce.

The authors analyzed a cohort of patients with autism spectrum disorder for mitochondrial disease. They compared features of those with confirmed mitochondrial problems against the wider group. The overlap suggests energy metabolism deserves a real place in the medical workup of autism.
plos-pone-0003915:
Lijan Lo, Zhenhai Zhang, Ni Hong, and co-authors catalogued gene activity in fish testes in 2008. Their PLOS ONE article concerns the medaka, a small lab fish. Medaka is the first vertebrate whose sperm production was fully run in a dish. Studying that process lacked good molecular markers for each stage.

The team gathered 3,640 distinct gene clusters active in the medaka testis. Such a catalogue lets labs mark stages of sperm formation precisely. Many testis genes are shared across fish and mammals, they note. The list can guide studies of fertility in species far beyond medaka.
plos-pone-0004015:
Jasen Lee Gilge, Michael Fisher, and Yuh-Cherng Chai studied protein changes under oxidant stress in 2008. Cells defend themselves against oxidants in several ways. One protein response attaches glutathione to reactive cysteine sites. That change forms mixed disulfides on many proteins.

Their PLOS ONE article used HEK 293 cells to test what drives the change. Both oxidants and non-oxidant shifts in thiol levels played roles. The work separates causes that earlier studies had mixed together. Clearer chemistry helps explain how cells sense and survive oxidative stress. The full report sits in PLOS ONE, free to read with all its data shown.
plos-pone-0004115:
James J. Bull and William R. Harcombe modeled nutrient sharing between microbes in 2009. Cross-feeding means species exchange nutrients with each other. It may start as waste sharing between neighbors. Or it may evolve as cooperation, like reciprocal altruism.

Their PLOS ONE article explores when cooperative cross-feeding can evolve. Population dynamics constrained that evolution in their models. Crowding and mixing decide whether sharers beat cheaters. The result helps explain the stable food webs seen in microbial communities. The study ran in PLOS ONE, an open journal read by labs around the world. It was printed in PLOS ONE, where the full text stays free to read.
plos-pone-0004215:
Sophie Lebrecht and colleagues published this psychology study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Implicit racial bias means attitudes toward other-race groups that sit outside conscious awareness. Alongside it sits the other-race effect: faces of other races are harder to tell apart than faces of one's own race.

The team asked whether perceptual training, practice at telling other-race faces apart, reduces implicit racial bias. Linking a perceptual skill to a social attitude would offer a new route to easing bias. The study tests whether learning to see faces as individuals changes how the mind judges a group.
plos-pone-0004315:
Isabel Martín Caballero and colleagues published this stem cell study in PLOS ONE in 2009. The molecular changes that occur when a neural stem cell switches from self-renewal to a committed lineage are not well understood. Control of gene expression clearly plays an important role in that switch, and DNA methylation is one of its tools.

The team examined three methyl-CpG binding proteins: Mecp2, Mbd2, and Kaiso. They report that these proteins are dispensable for mouse embryogenesis but play a redundant function in neural differentiation. Backup systems can hide a protein's importance until all the backups are removed.
plos-pone-0004415: In 2009, a French team scanned autistic children's brains for clues. MRI scans of 77 children with non-syndromic autism were carefully catalogued. The scans' real clinical value was weighed. The study tempers scan expectations in autism care. The scanning technology keeps improving fast.
plos-pone-0004515: In 2009, Church, Martin, and Thompson tested exercise doses for real weight loss. Different exercise doses shifted weight, waist, and compensatory responses measurably. The body fought back hard against big doses. The finding tempers workout expectations a bit. The test doses varied widely.
plos-pone-0004615: In 2009, a team fingerprinted hungry germ appetites anew. Trait fingerprinting showed that pure germ teams break down aromatics. The hungry germ teams broke down tough pollutants fast. The neat method aids biofuel research today. The key breakdown needs no air.
plos-pone-0004715: In 2009, Gaglio and a team starved cancer cells of glutamine anew. Glutamine starving stalled K-Ras cells until DNA parts rescued them. The fuel shortage halted copying cold here. The study maps cancer metabolism wiring. The fuel dependence is metabolic still today.
legge-forerunners-and-rivals-vol-2-1915:
Religions competed with early Christianity across the Roman world, and Francis Legge spent two volumes mapping the rivals. Forerunners and Rivals of Christianity, Volume Two, published in 1915, takes up the story from the year 330 backward and forward through the great systems. The Gnostic schools receive the deepest treatment here.

Valentinians, Basilideans, and Marcionites appear as serious religious thinkers rather than cartoon villains. Legge's sympathy for these so-called heretics set his history apart in its day. He traces how their ideas about creation, evil, and salvation challenged the young Church. Readers gain a fair hearing for voices mostly known through their enemies. The volume remains a humane guide to a tangled religious landscape.
jordanes-getica-mierow-1915:
Jordanes, a sixth-century writer, told the Goths' story in his Getica, here in Charles Mierow's 1915 English version. Origins, migrations, and kings fill his brisk Latin history. Attila's Huns, the Visigoths, and Rome's fall all pass through its pages.

Nearly all we know of early Gothic history flows through this one book. Jordanes drew on lost works, above all Cassiodorus's great history. His tale mixes legend, pride, and hard fact in equal parts. Mierow's version opened the text to English readers in clear form. It remains the most important barbarian history to survive from the age of migrations.
haslmayr-sendtschreiben-1615:
Adam Haslmayr answers the Rosicrucian manifestos in his Sendtschreiben, printed in German in 1615. The Tyrolean physician writes back to the unknown Brotherhood of the Rosy Cross with open joy. His letter, the first printed reply to the mysterious Fama, set all learned Europe buzzing with hope, doubt, and wild surmise.

Haslmayr begs the brethren to reveal themselves to a waiting world. He had already suffered prison for his alchemical faith and hopes. Enthusiasm, not irony, marks every line of his simple address. The pamphlet launched the strangest learned craze of the seventeenth century, the Rosicrucian furor, whose echoes ran for a hundred years.
jesuit-relations-thwaites-vol-15:
Volume 15, from 1898, follows the Hurons through 1638 and 1639. A strange pattern fills the reports that Thwaites prints here. Converts grow in number even while the plague years still cast a shadow.

The fathers' hope stays stubborn in the face of grim facts. Their letters home ring with trust that the mission will thrive. Modern readers know that hope is doomed, which sharpens each page. Baptisms, feasts, and new chapels mark a brief, bright season. The great chronicle keeps a steady beat as the storm builds offshore. Hope and dread share every report in this book.
journal-of-discourses-vol-15:
Panic on Wall Street shapes Volume Fifteen of the Journal, from 1873. Young answers hard times with the United Order, his boldest scheme. Saints are called to pool property and labor for the common good.

Cooperation rises, in his preaching, to the rank of God's own law. Towns across Utah try shared farms, shops, and herds under the plan. Sermons praise the order as Zion's shield against greed and want. A godly economy takes shape, for a time, in the desert. The volume shows faith turned into a full plan for daily life and work for all.
congress-of-vienna-final-act-1815:
After Napoleon's defeat, the great powers of Europe met at Vienna to redraw the continent's map. Their Final Act, signed in June 1815, gathered the whole settlement into one long document with many added treaties. Austria's Prince Metternich was the leading hand in the design, working beside the rulers of Russia, Prussia, and Britain.

The settlement moved borders, restored kings, and built a balance of power meant to stop any one nation from ruling Europe again. Smaller states were traded and merged with little regard for the wishes of their peoples. Even so, the Vienna order kept a general peace in Europe for decades and shaped diplomacy for a century.
bracton-de-legibus-woodbine-vol1-1915:
George Woodbine, a Yale legal scholar, opened a new critical edition of Bracton with a first volume in 1915. Bracton's De legibus is the great thirteenth-century treatise on the laws and customs of England. Woodbine went back to the manuscripts to improve on Twiss's Victorian text, which had served scholars since the 1880s.

The opening volume gives a fresh Latin text of the treatise's first part, with the manuscript evidence set out in detail. Woodbine studied how the work was copied and altered over time, which changed how later volumes were read. His edition aimed at accuracy where Twiss had sometimes guessed. The project set the modern standard for Bracton study, and scholars still cite Woodbine's text when the wording of the treatise matters.
savigny-geschichte-roem-rechts-ma-vol1-1:
Friedrich Carl von Savigny opened his History of Roman Law in the Middle Ages with a first volume in German in 1815. Savigny, a Berlin professor, asked what happened to Roman law in the centuries after Rome fell. The common story said it had vanished; his research showed it had lived on in cities, courts, and church practice.

Volume 1 traces the Corpus Juris through the early medieval centuries, following Roman law in Italy, France, and the German lands. Savigny works from charters, chronicles, and law books that few had read. The book founded the modern study of legal history and the historical school of law with it. Its motto, that law is a people's living spirit rather than a ruler's command, runs through the whole vast work that followed.
us-amendment-15:
Ratified in 1870, the Fifteenth Amendment closed the Reconstruction era with a promise about the ballot. Congress wrote it to stop states from keeping Black men from voting because of race. Its words also cover color and a past state of being held in slavery.

The text is short, but its meaning is large: the right to vote cannot be denied on those grounds. For decades after 1870, many states still blocked Black voters through tricks, tests, and fear. Only with the Voting Rights Act of 1965 did the promise gain real force. The amendment remains a core guard for voting rights.
cia-0000012315:
Someone was left alone for a few minutes in Buzinov's office, and a CIA document from January 1962 thought the moment worth recording. Buzinov was a Soviet official in the trade and science world the Penkovsky case moved through. In espionage, a few unguarded minutes in the right office can be worth months of patient work, and officers wrote such moments down.

The document preserves the vignette without the dressing of a finished report. Its brevity is its intrigue: who, what room, what seen, all compressed. For readers, it is a small human gap in the tradecraft, the kind great cases turn on.
cia-0000012415:
Meeting number thirty-five falls on September 27, 1961, near the Paris phase's peak. The sessions' intensity never flagged that month. By the thirty-fifth sitting, the count itself had become a measure of the operation's enormity. No source in memory had been worked this long, this often, or this deeply by two allied services acting as one team.

The record preserves the session's place in September's run. Handlers' notebooks filled while their source stayed willing and precise. For readers, the page shows momentum sustained across a season, in a city far from the danger waiting at home.
cia-0000013215:
Twelve years after the war ended, a Vietnamese official's comments on the POW and MIA issue were recorded in June 1987. The official spoke for the Socialist Republic of Vietnam, Hanoi's state. His words also touched on relations between Vietnam and the United States, the larger question into which the missing men had become permanently woven by then.

The record preserves Hanoi's late Cold War position in its own phrasing. The accounting was still unfinished, and both sides knew the issue blocked every other dealing. For readers, the page shows the war's longest aftermath still alive in diplomatic language.
cia-0000013615:
Peru's political prospects are weighed in a CIA paper from April 1963, in a season of generals and ballots. The military had seized power the year before to block an election result it disliked. New voting was promised, and the Andean republic's future hung on whether the soldiers would allow it. Parties, officers, and campesino movements all pressed their claims on the state at once.

The paper notes the generals' ambitions alongside the civilians' hopes. It treats the Andes' politics as the hemisphere's most volatile mixture. For readers, it shows Peru at one of its recurring crossroads, with Washington reading the signs.
cia-0000014715: Poland's government offered sanctuary to Julius and Ethel Rosenberg, in a CIA file dated May 1, 1952. The offer would have given the condemned couple a home abroad. Offers like it formed part of the worldwide campaign around their case. The file shows how even exile plans for two prisoners in New York became Cold War news.
cia-0000015315: A letter to Lloyd Berkner from Philip Strong fills a CIA file dated April 4, 1958. It concerns Leon Davidson's possible move, per the clipped title. Berkner got the same word sent to Page, Goudsmit, and Alvarez that day. The spread shows one amateur's claims treated as a matter for the top of science.
cia-0000021515: Capture of an American pilot in Xieng Khouang Province in mid 1970 leads a CIA record dated in 1971. The title's second item begins with an observation, then breaks off in the catalog. Xieng Khouang held the Plain of Jars, a much fought over part of Laos. One capture there joined hundreds of cases tracked by the prisoner offices.
cia-0000039115:
First Lieutenant Gerald Francis Kinsman is the subject of a CIA record dated February 2, 1971. The title notes that a first document in the file also mentions the execution of two men. Kinsman's own case stands at the head of the record.

Inside, the file concerns the lieutenant and the grave matter mentioned beside his name. Records that join a named officer to an execution report are among the hardest in the set. The file preserves what was known and reported at the time. Later readers must weigh a case that mixes one man's fate with a report of killings in the same pages.
cia-0000044015:
Possible FMLN links to the priests' murder were suggested, in a CIA record dated January 2, 1990. The title ties the suggestion to the Farabundo Marti National Liberation Front. The suggestion ran against the charge most voices laid on the army.

Inside, the counter-claim is preserved as it was put forward. Blaming the rebels served the government's friends at a hard moment. Few outside that circle credited the idea for long. The file keeps the attempt on record anyway, since the struggle over blame was itself part of the case's history from its earliest days onward.
cia-0000044415:
The foreign minister accused the FMLN of killing the priests, in a CIA record dated October 4, 1989 in the catalog. This file stands beside a companion record with a nearly matching title. Two filings of one charge show how widely it was pushed.

Inside, the accusation is recorded again, for a further audience. Repetition was the method: say it in every capital that would listen. The government's friends abroad needed the counter-story in hand. The file preserves that effort's second trace, and with it the shape of a campaign to move blame before any court had heard a word of evidence.
cia-0000045215:
Officials hoped the kidnapping situation would become more clear in 24 hours, in a CIA record dated September 2, 1985. A one-day promise is a hostage to fortune in any crisis. The kidnappers, not the officials, held the real timetable that week.

Inside, the short-lived optimism of that forecast is preserved. Deadlines in kidnapping cases are set to calm the public. They are just as often missed, to the government's cost. The file holds one such promise at its making, a small and human record of hope spoken aloud in a crisis that refused to follow anyone's schedule.
cia-0000047315:
Studies in Intelligence was the CIA's own professional journal, written by officers for officers, and this entry holds its winter 1974 issue, volume 18, number 4. The issue's named piece treats General de Gaulle in action. De Gaulle, France's wartime leader and later president, dealt with American intelligence across three decades.

Inside, the journal's pages carry the trade talking to itself: methods, history, and lessons drawn from past operations. A study of de Gaulle fit that mission, since few foreign leaders had tested American spies so often. Declassified long after printing, the issue now shows readers how the agency studied its craft from within.
cia-0000049315: Briefing Senator Leahy on Panama and El Salvador is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000049315, dated January 1, 1990. The record concerns a briefing given to Senator Leahy covering two countries, Panama and El Salvador. It survives as a short declassified note of the session, useful mainly as evidence that the briefing took place and what ground it covered.
cia-0000049415: El Salvador requests extradition of Hans Christ is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000049415, dated May 3, 1981, filed under an international terrorism weekly heading. The item records a formal request naming Christ. It survives as a short declassified notice of that request, useful for the named person and the legal step stated in its title.

Charles Francis Adams sent this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 18 December 1862. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 15 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

By mid-December the talk in London had cooled on stepping into the war, and Adams's mail charted that shift. He wrote of the cabinet, the papers, and the men who spoke for the South in Britain. Each report helped Seward judge how much risk lay across the sea. This dispatch is a mid-run piece of that watch, plain in tone and rich in use when read with the rest.
frus-1863p1-d115:
Three letters to London on 11 March 1863 close with this note from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 115 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

The third sheet of a set often carried the day's last word: a small order, a tone to hold, a fact just in. Seward's close of 11 March is in that place. The run of his March letters shows a secretary driving the London brief hard as spring came on. Twelve came in a day, then three more. This letter is the tail of that drive.
frus-1863p1-d215: Secretary of State William H. Seward sent this instruction to Charles Francis Adams, his minister in London, on 18 June 1863. It is document 215 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, within the orders that steered American policy toward Britain during the Civil War. Through such letters Washington told its man in London what to press, protest, or let pass.
frus-1863p1-d315:
To Mr. Stuart of the British legation in Washington, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote on 3 November 1862. The note is document 315 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress.

Britain had taken a neutral stand in 1861, and its legation in Washington guarded that stand case by case. A note like this one is neutrality being practiced, not just proclaimed. The letter's value lies partly in its place in the sequence: it shows the conversation between the two capitals continuing without a break.
frus-1863p1-d415:
Frederick W. Seward, Assistant Secretary of State, addressed this note to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, on 14 March 1863. It is document 415 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad.

The younger Seward often signed for the department when his father, the Secretary, was absent. Notes to Lyons still carried the full weight of the American position on neutral rights and British complaints. Lyons reported the exchange to London, so each reply spoke to two audiences. The channel stayed busy because small disputes, left alone, could grow into a breach between the two countries.
frus-1863p1-d515:
Under the date 15 May 1863, the record holds a letter from Secretary William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington. The two men at the ends of this channel, Seward in Washington and Lyons speaking for Britain, wrote to each other almost daily. It appears in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department volume printed with the President's annual message for 1863.

For historians, the value lies in the run of the letters. Together they trace, almost day by day, how the Union kept its most dangerous foreign problem from boiling over. Much of the mail between the two offices turned on ships: the Union blockade, seized cargoes, and Confederate agents buying vessels in British ports. Alone it is one note among hundreds. In place, it is part of how a war stayed between the two sides that started it.
frus-1863p1-d615:
From F. W. Seward, the assistant secretary to Britain's chargé d'affaires William Stuart: a letter dated 18 August 1863. Stuart was holding the British legation in Washington while Lord Lyons was away on leave, so the channel ran through him that season. The letter was later printed in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message.

What the page shows is process, not drama. Claims, protests, and replies moved back and forth until small disputes stayed small. Students of the war use this mail to see foreign policy as the men on the spot lived it, page by page. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
plos-pbio-0020015:
Jun R. Huh, Stephanie Y. Vernooy, Hong Yu, and co-workers studied sperm formation in the fruit fly for PLOS Biology in 2004. Caspases are enzymes best known for driving cell death. Yet in fly testes, they help shape sperm in a process that splits a shared mass into single sperm cells.

The surprise is that death enzymes do careful building work here without killing the cell. The team found that more than one caspase chain is needed for sperm to separate properly. That means the system has backup and fine control, not a single switch. The study broadens what caspases are for. It hints that other tissues may also borrow death tools for safe, local tasks.
plos-pone-0000115:
Ashraf Yusuf Rangrez, Kannayakanahalli Maheshwarappa Dayananda, Santosh Atanur, and colleagues report this microbiology study in PLOS ONE in 2006. They searched the bacterium Aeromonas culicicola for a type four secretion system. This is a molecular machine bacteria use during conjugation, the process of passing DNA to a neighbor cell.

Finding such machinery matters because conjugation spreads genes, including ones for drug resistance, between bacteria. The authors report detecting the parts of this system in this species. The result adds a data point to the map of which bacteria carry the tools for gene swapping, and how those tools are built.
plos-pone-0000215:
Marie-dominique Franco, Jonathan Bohbot, Kenny Fernandez, and colleagues published this insect neuroscience paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. In the moth Manduca sexta, the olfactory epithelium lines the antennae and holds the smell-sensing cells. The authors study how sensory cells proliferate, keep being born, within that tissue as the moth develops into an adult.

A moth's sense of smell guides it to food and mates, and its sensors are renewed over life. Tracking where new sensory cells come from explains how the system stays sharp. The work adds to the study of adult neurogenesis, the birth of new nerve cells in mature animals.
plos-pone-0000315:
Chen Chen, Jiaqi Tang, Wei Dong, and colleagues published this genomics paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Streptococcus suis is a pig bacterium that can infect people and, rarely, cause streptococcal toxic shock syndrome. The authors compare the genomes of two Chinese isolates of S. suis 2 to get a glimpse of what makes such strains dangerous.

China had seen human outbreaks of this syndrome, so the isolates mattered beyond pig farming. Comparing their genomes with milder strains highlights candidate virulence genes. The study is an early example of using comparative genomics to investigate an emerging zoonotic threat.
plos-pone-0000415:
Frank Powilleit, Tanja Breinig, and Manfred J. Schmitt turned a yeast virus's shell into a building platform, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. The L-A virus of yeast wraps itself in a protein capsid. The team used that capsid inside living yeast to assemble chimeric virus-like particles, shells that mix the original protein with foreign pieces.

Virus-like particles are prized in vaccine work because they look like viruses to the immune system but cannot cause infection. A yeast-based assembly line could make them cheaply, and the same platform can display foreign proteins for research. The study is a piece of bioengineering: borrowing a virus's carpentry for human purposes.
plos-pone-0000515:
Liam J. Drew and colleagues identified pain channels that a sea snail toxin can block, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. The channels are high-threshold mechanosensitive ion channels, opened by strong pressure, and they mediate pressure-evoked pain. A novel conopeptide, a small toxin from a cone snail, blocked them.

Pressure pain is hard to treat because the channels responsible were poorly defined. A selective blocker is both a research probe and a possible drug lead: cone snail toxins have already yielded one approved pain medicine. Naming the channel and its blocker together moves mechanical pain from a vague complaint toward a molecular target.
plos-pone-0000615:
Sharon J. Sequeira, Aparna C. Ranganathan, Alejandro P. Adam and co-authors studied a stress pathway inside breast cells for PLOS ONE in 2007. When the endoplasmic reticulum, the cell's protein-folding workshop, is under stress, a kinase called PERK switches on. PERK acts on a protein named eIF2α and slows new protein making.

That slowdown can halt the cell cycle or push a cell toward death, limiting growth. The team links this control of cell division to two outcomes. One is how mammary acinar structures, the small sacs of the breast, take shape. The other is how tumors form. Cancer researchers will note the bridge between cell stress and tumor growth.
plos-pone-0000715:
John T. Schousboe, Kevin E. Wilson and Thomas N. Hangartner asked whether one scan can catch two dangers in older women. Their 2007 PLOS ONE study starts from a stark fact: cardiovascular disease is the most common cause of death among post-menopausal women. Their objective was to test lateral spine images taken on a bone densitometer, a machine used to detect vertebral fractures.

Could those same images accurately detect calcification of the abdominal aorta, a warning sign for heart disease? The comparison standard was digital radiography. If fracture-assessment images reveal aortic calcium too, a routine bone check gains heart value at no extra radiation or cost. Screening efficiency matters most in busy clinics.
plos-pone-0000815:
Michelle S. Lewis, Diane J. Pikaard, Mikhail Nasrallah and colleagues pinpointed where one parent's ribosomal genes get silenced in hybrids. In a genetic hybrid, silencing of one parental set of rRNA genes is an epigenetic phenomenon called nucleolar dominance. The team had shown silencing stays within the nucleolus organizer regions. Those are the loci where rRNA genes sit in tandem repeats. Silencing does not spread beyond them.

Their 2007 PLOS ONE study pursues that locus-specific silencing. Ribosomal RNA genes are needed in huge numbers, yet hybrids switch off a whole parental set. How a cell chooses and silences one array, precisely at its locus, is a clean model for epigenetic control of repeated genes.
plos-pone-0000915:
Michael Akhras, Magnus Unemo, Sreedevi Thiyagarajan and colleagues built a one primer system that copies many DNA targets at once, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Their method grows out of an older assay called the molecular inversion probe. The team added a complete gap filling step to make it stronger.

They call the result connector inversion probe technology. As a proof of concept, they show it can amplify many chosen sequences in a single reaction. Copying many targets at once, cleanly, is the backbone of genetic testing and pathogen hunting. A flexible system like this can serve labs that need wide screens from small samples.
plos-pone-0001015:
Simone Macri, Paolo Pasquali, Luca Bonsignore and colleagues found that mild stress in newborn mice made adults more alike, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Animal studies of human illness are trusted only if other labs can repeat them. The team note that claim often fails under varied housing and test conditions.

Working under their own lab conditions, they report that moderate neonatal stress decreased variation within groups in behavior, immunity and stress hormone responses. A treatment that tightens results could make mouse studies easier to repeat. It also raises a subtle point: the earliest days of life may set how uniform a lab population stays.
plos-pone-0001115:
Genes are switched on and off by proteins called transcription factors, which bind to short stretches of DNA near their target genes. Stein Aerts and colleagues tackle a basic puzzle in this field in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. From DNA patterns alone, can one predict which genes a given factor will control?

The team works on refining enhancer models, the computer models that score likely binding sites and regulatory regions. Their aim is a method that holds up across several genomes, not just one species. Better predictions would help researchers map the wiring of gene networks without testing every gene in the lab.
plos-pone-0001215:
Arteriosclerosis, the hardening and narrowing of arteries, is a common cause of chronic illness and death. Marcus Mutschelknauss, Marco Kummer, and Juergen Muser took on a diagnostic gap in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Heart attacks and strokes reveal vulnerable patients only after damage is done. Biomarkers to spot them in advance were lacking.

The authors propose scoring each person's arteriosclerosis by empiric clinical profiling, building a risk profile from a patient's clinical features. Finding vulnerable patients before a cardiovascular event is the real prize, since prevention then has time to work. Their approach uses plain clinical data rather than exotic tests.
plos-pone-0001315:
Bacteria of the class 1 integron type shuffle antibiotic resistance genes like cards, catching and using gene cassettes. Véronique Dubois and colleagues present a new lab assay for the enzyme that does the shuffling, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The enzyme, IntI1 integrase, is a tyrosine recombinase.

Recent data had shown that its recombination acts on the bottom strand of the attC site, but the exact mechanism stayed unclear. The authors' in vitro strand transfer assay lets researchers monitor IntI1 activity directly. Such an assay supports work on slowing the spread of antibiotic resistance.
plos-pone-0001415:
Jian Duan and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE review that pools past trials of farm crops and honey bees. Bees are the top pollinators for many crops world wide. They are also a key test species when new pest proof crops are judged for safety. Some feared that such crops could harm bees.

The authors combined data from many prior studies into one pooled analysis. Pooling gives a firmer verdict than any single small trial. Their work weighs the proof on bee harm from crops that make their own pest toxin. The verdict helps regulators and farmers judge real risk as these crops spread.
plos-pone-0001515:
Emma Underwood and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on how to spend wild life funds with care. The usual rule favors species hotspots, dense zones packed with species. But dense does not always mean the best value for money spent. The team set cost into the choice in a formal way.

Their method weighs species saved per dollar spent in each region. Some less dense zones win on that scale. The result urges funders to count cost, not just species tallies. With funds tight, return on spend may save more life in the end than hotspot habit alone.
plos-pone-0001615:
Simon Ho, Urmas Saarma, and Ross Barnett wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a pitfall in dating species pasts. Dates drawn from gene data guide much of ecology: they link species splits to past climate and gauge how fast new species form. Those dates rest on calibration points, past facts used to set the clock. The team show what goes wrong when a point is mis set.

Through three case studies, wrong points bend dates by a wide margin. The bends can flip the tale a study tells. Their work is a caution and a check list for the field. Sound dates are the spine of any claim about how life changed over time.
plos-pone-0001715:
Daniel E. Rozen, Michelle G. J. L. Habets, Andreas Handel, and their co-authors tested a textbook claim about small populations in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Small populations are thought to adapt poorly. Harmful mutations hurt them more, and they have limited access to new helpful mutations, above all those with large benefits. Complex fitness landscapes, where many peaks and valleys separate good and bad gene combinations, should make this worse.

The team tracked how small populations actually evolved on such landscapes. Their title promises heterogeneous trajectories: the populations did not all follow one path. The full text gives the evolution experiments and the routes found. Results like these refine when small populations are truly stuck and when they can still climb.
plos-pone-0001815:
Ingrid B. Müller, Julia Knöckel, Matthew R. Groves, and their co-authors studied vitamin B6 production in the malaria parasite in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Plants, fungi, bacteria, and the apicomplexan parasite Plasmodium falciparum can synthesize vitamin B6 themselves, while mammals must take it in from diet. Its active form is pyridoxal 5-phosphate, or PLP.

The team shows the assembly of the plasmodial PLP synthase complex follows a defined course. The full text gives the protein interaction steps and structures. Because humans cannot make B6, the parasite's synthesis machinery is a clean drug target. Blocking it should starve the parasite without touching the host's supply route.
plos-pone-0001915:
Nicholas Funderburg and co-authors studied how germ signals affect the T cells lost in HIV, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. People with chronic HIV show high levels of germ products in the blood, leaked from the gut. That leak has been linked to a fired-up immune system and to loss of CD4 T cells, the cells HIV destroys.

The team exposed human T cells to signals that trip Toll-like receptors, the cell alarms for germ parts. They tracked both activation and death of the cells. Their model may show one way HIV keeps the immune system both overactive and depleted at once, a core riddle of the illness.
plos-pone-0002015:
Beatriz Quinones and co-authors compared the genomes of a gut bacterium's strains from South Africa, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Campylobacter jejuni is a common cause of acute diarrhea and is also tied to later nerve ills, Guillain-Barre and Miller Fisher syndromes. Around Cape Town, strains of one heat-stable serotype, HS:41, have been noted.

The team set clinical strains from South Africa side by side at the genome level. Shared and distinct genes can hint why some strains cause nerve harm after gut infection. Regional genome data also help health labs track which strains circulate near Cape Town.
plos-pone-0002115:
Sokol Todi and co-authors used the fruit fly to study a motor protein vital to hearing, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Myosin VIIA is an unconventional motor protein necessary for hearing in vertebrates. In human ears, sound is caught by sensory hair cells whose tops carry staircase-like bundles of protrusions called stereocilia, and Myosin VIIA maintains those bundles.

As the title states, the protein is necessary for the development of the auditory organ in the fly Drosophila. A fly ear built on the same motor lets labs test hearing genes fast, in an animal that is cheap to breed.
plos-pone-0002215:
Seiko Oda, Tomoyuki Oda, Kenichiro Nishi, and co-authors linked an inflammation protein to a growth signal in low-oxygen cells, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The protein, macrophage migration inhibitory factor or MIF, acts in inflammation and also has hormone and enzyme roles. It had been tied to tumor growth as well.

Tumors often outgrow their blood supply and turn on a factor called HIF, which helps cells survive with little oxygen. The team reports that MIF switches on HIF, and that this step depends on p53, a famous tumor suppressor. The link ties inflammation, oxygen sensing, and cancer into one chain of events.
plos-pone-0002315:
Chitralekha Bhattacharya, Sita Aggarwal, Madhu Kumar, and co-authors studied a mouse protein family in germ cells, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The dead-end gene, Dnd1, is essential for keeping germ cells alive; without it, animals become sterile and develop testicular tumors. Its protein binds the tail region of messenger RNAs and can shield them from microRNA attack.

The team examined the mouse APOBEC3 protein, known from antiviral defense, and found it is expressed in germ cells and interacts with DND1. A partnership between an RNA editor and an RNA guardian in germ cells could shape which messages survive to build eggs and sperm.
plos-pone-0002415:
Jelluma joined co-authors to publish a research article in PLOS ONE in 2008. Named on the byline are Nannette Jelluma, Arjan B. Brenkman, Ian McLeod, among others. Its subject is chromosomal Instability by Inefficient Mps1 Auto-Activation Due to a Weakened Mitotic Checkpoint and Lagging Chromosomes. Chromosomal instability (CIN), a feature widely shared by cells from solid tumors, is caused by occasional chromosome missegregations during cell division.

The authors lay out their aims in clear terms and keep the focus on the work itself. In short, the piece gives a clear, short route into a field that can seem hard to enter from the outside.
plos-pone-0002515:
Bafna led the team behind a 2008 research article in PLOS ONE. Named on the byline are Pallavi A. Bafna, Prasad G. Purohit, Anthony Auerbach, among others. Its subject is gating at the Mouth of the Acetylcholine Receptor Channel: Energetic Consequences of Mutations in the αM2-Cap.

The writing stays close to the facts the team had in hand when the work was done. For science readers, it shows how a small, well framed question can add a firm piece of knowledge to a much larger field. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002615:
Yamaza and other authors present their study in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. Named on the byline are Takayoshi Yamaza, Yasuo Miura, Yanming Bi, among others. Its subject is pharmacologic Stem Cell Based Intervention as a New Approach to Osteoporosis Treatment in Rodents. Osteoporosis is the most prevalent skeletal disorder, characterized by a low bone mineral density (BMD) and bone structural deterioration, leading to bone fragility fractures.

The authors lay out their aims in clear terms and keep the focus on the work itself. Readers finish with a clear sense of the problem, the approach, and why the question was worth the team's time.
plos-pone-0002715:
Teresa Lopardo and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was claudin-1 is a p63 target gene with a crucial role in epithelial development. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Teresa Lopardo, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. The epidermis of the skin is a self-renewing, stratified epithelium that functions as the interface between the human body and the outer environment. Readers get a clear record of the question, the approach named in the abstract, and the context the authors give for the work.
plos-pone-0002815:
Timothy S. Ham and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was design and construction of a double inversion recombination switch for heritable sequential genetic memory. The catalog record names Timothy S. Ham first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. Inversion recombination elements present unique opportunities for computing and information encoding in biological systems. The piece stands as a short, open record of the research question and the grounds on which the authors pursued it. No results or figures are claimed in this summary beyond what the title and abstract themselves state.
plos-pone-0002915:
Takeshi Hashimoto, Rajaa Hussien, Hyung-Sook Cho and co-authors looked for a lactate-burning system inside rat neurons in 2008. Lactate is often cast as a waste product, yet brain cells may pass it between them as fuel. That passing idea is called a lactate shuttle.

The team checked whether transporter proteins MCT1 and MCT2 and the enzyme LDH sit together in neuron mitochondria. Finding them there would support an intracellular shuttle inside the neuron itself. Published in PLOS ONE, the study backs that complex with direct evidence, reshaping how brain energy use is pictured. Anyone can read the full text free of charge through the journal's open access site.
plos-pone-0003015:
Scott Fitzpatrick, Greg Nelson and Geoffrey Clark disputed claims of dwarf prehistoric people on Palau in 2008. The western Micronesian islands were settled around 3,000 to 3,300 years ago. Recent claims had suggested the settlers shrank through insular dwarfism, the island trend toward smaller body size.

Biological and archaeological data indicate the inhabitants were normal sized, the authors argue, despite small scattered bone fragments. Published in PLOS ONE, the title makes the verdict plain. The case is a warning about building a dramatic human story on fragmentary remains. Anyone can read the full text free of charge through the journal's open access site.
plos-pone-0003115:
Joana Borlido, Greg Veltri, Antony Jackson and co-authors tested clathrin's role at the mitotic spindle in 2008. Clathrin is a multi-part protein involved in vesicle coat assembly, the cell's shipping system. Recently its distribution was reported to change during the cell cycle, with clathrin found at the spindle that separates chromosomes.

Recruitment to the spindle might mean an essential mitotic job, or mere association. The title gives the verdict: clathrin is spindle-associated but not essential for mitosis. Published in PLOS ONE, separating presence from necessity is a useful discipline for cell biology claims. Full methods, data, and references appear in the complete article for readers who want more detail.
plos-pone-0003215:
Yau-Hua Yu, Hsu-Ko Kuo and Kuo-Wei Chang review gene expression work on a head and neck cancer in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Numerous studies were performed to illuminate mechanisms of tumour formation and spread from gene expression profiles of head and neck squamous cell carcinoma. The objective of this review is to conduct a network-based meta-analysis to identify the underlying biological themes.

Readers get many single studies combined into one evolving transcriptome picture. A meta-analysis can show which signals repeat across labs and which were local noise. For a cancer with varied courses, shared network themes may point to more reliable markers.
plos-pone-0003315:
Chris Rae and co-authors test virus shells as tiny building blocks in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Cowpea mosaic virus is used more and more as a nanoparticle base: chemists attach many copies of a molecule to its outer shell. Uses range from sensors to drug carriers. Work with live virus, though, raises safety worries for such uses.

The team check whether virus particles killed by ultraviolet light can still be chemically addressed, tagged at set sites on the shell. Readers learn if dead particles keep the useful surface traits. Safe, inert shells are what virus-based nano tools need for real use.
plos-pone-0007415: Cancer drugs often fail because tumors learn to pump them out — multidrug resistance — and no safe fix has ever reached patients. In a large cell-based screen, the researchers discovered a compound called NSC23925 that restores the drugs' power. The molecule reverses the resistance mechanism itself rather than just adding more poison, offering a genuinely new strategy for failed chemotherapy.
plos-pone-0007515: To copy its DNA, the ulcer-causing bacterium Helicobacter pylori unwinds the double helix with a motor protein called DnaB helicase. This study solved the 3D shape of the motor's front end and mapped how it grips its partner, the primase. Seeing the connection in atomic detail exposes a potential target for new antibiotics.
plos-pone-0007615: Tuberculosis bacteria secrete a protein called ESAT6 that helps them cause disease. This study designed short phenylalanine-rich peptides that latch onto ESAT6 and, in doing so, slow the pathogen's growth. Targeting a secreted virulence factor is a fresh angle for fighting a bacterium that kills over a million people a year.
plos-pone-0007715: Colon tumors with unstable DNA often lose genes to mutation. This study screened such tumors and found frequent mutations in the tail end of RB1CC1, a gene that normally restrains growth. The previously overlooked region emerges as a casualty of the tumor's genetic chaos.
plos-pone-0007815: Look-alike germs got a sequencing verdict. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Comas's team showed DNA sequencing beats old typing for clone-like TB. Old methods lean on jumpy DNA bits. The verdict was logged. The check feeds disease tracking.
plos-pone-0007915: Lesser scaup ducks are declining, but where do the harvested birds come from? This study used stable isotopes in feathers to trace North American scaup to their breeding grounds. The isotopic map gives conservationists the origins they need to act.
plos-pone-0008015: Owls pinpoint sound by multiplying two cues — timing and loudness differences between ears. This study showed a hierarchy of population codes creates those multiplicative receptive fields in the owl's midbrain. The neural math behind a predator's precision hearing gets a formal model.
plos-pone-0008115: A plant compound's cancer trick was traced to cell-surface chemistry. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Skalska and colleagues proposed that the sesquiterpene lactone parthenolide acts by modulating free thiols on cell-surface proteins. Targeting redox pathways is a promising cancer strategy. The surface-thiol mechanism offers a new explanation for the compound's effects.
plos-pone-0008215: Cattle TB tests were graded in Chad. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Muller's team used Bayesian methods to judge multiple diagnostic tests for bovine tuberculosis in Chadian cattle. The disease blankets Africa, yet good data on test accuracy are scarce. The head-to-head evaluation shows which tests to trust. The results guide TB control where resources are thinnest.
plos-pone-0008315: A heparin antidote was found tuning heart calcium channels. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Diaz-Sylvester's team showed protamine modulates cardiac ryanodine receptors (RyR2) in a voltage-dependent way. The drug was known to block skeletal-muscle channels. The heart-channel tests extend the picture. The modulation matters where protamine meets cardiac care.
plos-pone-0008415: A hunger brain signal was found building bone. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Baldock's team showed neuropeptide Y knockout mice reveal NPY's role in matching bone mass to body weight. Brain energy sensing steers the skeleton. Without NPY, the match breaks. The brain-bone axis opens new osteoporosis angles.
plos-pone-0008515: Wound healing's paradox got a computer referee. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Sun's team modeled TGF-beta1's conflicting roles in skin wound healing with a 3D epidermis simulation. The factor both speeds and stalls skin cells. The model reconciles the clash. The virtual referee clarifies the healing playbook.
plos-pone-0008615: A brain virus got an RNA-interference shield. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Kumar and Arankalle showed P-gene siRNA in the brain protects mice from lethal Chandipura virus encephalitis. The pediatric killer claims 55 to 75 percent of victims. The RNA shield worked. The result offers hope for a treatment.
plos-pone-0008715: A brain receptor's tail got a docking check. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Coleman's team analyzed the GluA4 carboxyl-terminus role in PDZ interactions. The AMPA receptor's synaptic delivery needed mapping. The tail's docking role was decoded. The check refines synapse biology.
plos-pone-0008815: Memory immune cells' signal got a boost. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Man's team showed IgG-BCR augments B-cell antigen responses without antigen-induced signaling. The augmented response was mapped. The boost reveals immune memory mechanics.
plos-pone-0008915: Model knobs' knowability got a rulebook. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Little's team wrote the rules for which model knobs can be known from data. The unknowable-knob problem was formalized. The rulebook keeps modelers straight.
plos-pone-0009015: HIV shots got a DNA-prime boost. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Koup's team showed DNA priming augments adenoviral-vector HIV vaccine antibody and T-cell responses. The prime-boost regimen was tested. The boost advances HIV vaccines.
plos-pone-0009115: Human mate-copying got a gaze test. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Yorzinski and Platt showed same-sex gaze attraction influences mate-choice copying in humans. The gaze-tracking experiment was run. The test informs evolutionary psychology.
plos-pone-0009215: Flu checks got a bedside playbook. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Nougairede's team wrote a bedside playbook for fast flu checks in hospitals. The playbook was tested. The playbook speeds outbreak response. The playbook ran in Marseille hospitals.
plos-pone-0009315: An anxiety gene was tested for arthritis links. This 2010 PLOS ONE study by D'Amato and colleagues analyzed neuropeptide S receptor gene polymorphisms in rheumatoid arthritis. While NPSR1 variants were associated with asthma and inflammatory bowel disease, and the receptor modulates anxiety in the brain, its arthritis role was unknown. The genetic analysis tests whether a brain-gut-immune gene also shapes joint disease.
plos-pone-0011415: Children raised in severely neglectful institutions carry the damage in their brain waves — but does rescue timing matter? This research paper measures brain electrical activity in children exposed to extreme psychosocial neglect, comparing earlier versus later intervention. The results show when help arrives shapes the recovering brain, strengthening the case for placing vulnerable children in family care as early as possible.
plos-pone-0011515: APOBEC3G is a human protein that wrecks HIV, but its 3D shape looked different in crystals than in solution. This research paper runs computer simulations of the molecule's motion to bridge the two pictures. The merged view explains the clash and hands drug designers a truer image of an anti-HIV guard.
plos-pone-0011615: Hepatitis B has deep roots in rural Nigeria, but its history was unwritten. This research paper reconstructs the epidemic history and evolutionary dynamics of the virus in two remote communities. The viral family tree reveals how the infection spread and changed in isolation.
